title: Pardons Angela Stanton
description_medium: On February 18, 2020, President Donald Trump granted Angela Ronae Stanton a full pardon. Stanton had been convicted in federal court in Georgia for her role in a stolen-vehicle ring and served six months of home confinement. The White House cited her later work as an author, television personality and criminal-justice reform advocate, particularly her efforts to improve reentry for people returning from prison.
description_long:
The Justice Department’s clemency record identifies Stanton’s federal case in the Northern District of Georgia. It lists a 2007 conviction for conspiracy involving interstate transportation of a stolen motor vehicle and tampering with a vehicle identification number. Her sentence was time served and three years of supervised release, including six months of home confinement.

Trump granted Stanton a full pardon on February 18, 2020, alongside six other pardons and four commutations. The distinction is significant: Stanton received a pardon, while several other people announced that day had prison terms shortened. The White House presented Stanton’s post-conviction work as its rationale, describing her as an author and television personality who advocated criminal-justice reform and worked to improve reentry for people leaving prison. It also identified Alveda King as a supporter of the grant. The clemency announcement did not claim that Stanton’s conviction was mistaken; it framed the pardon as recognition of her later rehabilitation and community work.
source_access_notes: Read Stanton’s DOJ pardon instrument and the archived White House announcement, which names the full pardon, sentence, rehabilitation rationale and supporter.
rationale: DOJ establishes the offense and sentence; the White House supplies the stated reasons for clemency and distinguishes Stanton’s full pardon from same-day commutations.

title: Matthew Charles was released under the First Step Act, not a Trump commutation
description_medium: Matthew Charles was returned to federal prison in 2018 after a judge reversed an earlier sentence reduction. His lawyers and advocates sought presidential clemency, but he was released in January 2019 after the First Step Act became law and he was resentenced to time served.
description_long:
Matthew Charles’s case drew national attention in 2018 after he was sent back to prison. Sentenced in 1996 to 35 years for drug and firearms offenses, he served 21 years before a sentence reduction let him out in 2016. A judge later determined that the reduction had been based on an incomplete record and ordered him to serve the remainder. Advocates, including his pro bono lawyer Shon Hopwood, petitioned for presidential clemency while also working for broader sentencing reform.

Charles’s release came through a different route: after Trump signed the First Step Act in December 2018, a federal court resentenced him to time served, and he left prison on January 3, 2019, the first person released under the law. The Justice Department’s Trump commutations list does not include him. His release drew attention from criminal-justice advocates who had pressed for sentencing reform.

corrected_wording.original: Commutes Sentence of Mathew G. Charles
corrected_wording.replacement: Matthew Charles was released under the First Step Act, not a Trump commutation
corrected_wording.reason: The public record does not support describing Matthew Charles as a recipient of a Trump commutation.

source_access_notes: Justice Department commutation list checked for the recipient; CBS News read for the sentence-reduction reversal and clemency advocacy; Georgetown Law read for First Step Act resentencing and release.
blockers: The assigned name “Mathew G. Charles” does not match the public case name “Matthew Charles,” and no DOJ commutation entry confirms a presidential grant to either spelling.
rationale: The named commutation is unsupported: the DOJ list has no Matthew Charles entry, and contemporary reporting says his release followed First Step Act resentencing. The assigned middle initial/name differs from that public case name, so identity remains uncertain.
